en: The Extensive Ritual Manual of the Mahāvairocana Sūtra, Volume One;
also titled the *Mahākaruṇā-garbha-vyūha*.
Homage to the Buddha Vairocana, whose pure eyes are blossomed like blue lotuses.
Relying upon the teachings of the *Mahāvairocana Sūtra*, I shall explain the various ritual procedures for making offerings;
by following them, one shall attain swift accomplishment.
Yet, the initial accomplishment of the benefit of oneself and others—the means of the supreme wisdom and vows—arises from the power of faith and understanding that initiates *siddhi*.
The supreme sons born of all Tathāgatas, who embody the mantras and forms of those Buddhas,
abide in various mudrās and majestic postures; they have profound faith in the path of the sublime mantras and the Vaipulya vehicle,
and out of compassion for the beings wandering through the six realms of saṃsāra, [they practice].
He expounds [the teachings] for the sake of conformity and benefit;
he also gives rise to diligent sincerity and deep faith, knowing the practice of subduing through sublime mantras,
and understanding the various constituent parts that comprise the necessary conditions.
Seeing such a teacher, I pay him respectful homage, Gazing up at him as if he were the Teacher of the World.
I provide for him with offerings and service according to his needs, Complying well with the teacher’s intent to bring him joy.
Bowing my head, I entreat the supreme Sugata to proceed; I pray that the Honored One will instruct me as is appropriate.
That master, acting with sovereign ease, establishes the wondrous and perfect mandalas such as the Mahākaruṇā-garbha;
according to the ritual, he summons [the deities] into the maṇḍala and, in accordance with the disciples' capacities, bestows the samaya,
the fundamental mantras of the practice site, and the mudrās.
According to one's own capacity and in accordance with what is appropriate, one should invite and make offerings to all;
toward the teacher who bestows the precepts and those of the same holy life, one must never harbor thoughts of disparagement or destruction.
Next, one should pay homage to the Honored One who confers empowerment and transmits the teachings, and request the mantras for the practice to be cultivated.
Once the wise practitioner has received the master’s authorization, they should establish a maṇḍala according to the Dharma in a location appropriate to the specific site,
while always remaining fully endowed with patience and wisdom.
Whether with a pure and virtuous companion or alone, one should be accompanied by the volumes of the sublime Dharma;
thus achieving accomplishment for oneself and others in this present life, and relying on no other gods out of fear—
one who possesses these qualities is called a noble assistant.
Each day, first abide in mindfulness and wisdom; when rising from sleep according to the Dharma, eliminate all obstacles that are inexhaustible.
With a sincere heart, contemplate the Buddhas of the ten directions, and facing the direction where your chosen deity resides, prostrate with the five limbs touching the ground.
I take refuge in the Perfectly Awakened Ones of the ten directions, In all those of the three times who possess the three bodies;
I take refuge in the entirety of the Mahāyāna Dharma, And in the assembly of those who do not regress from Bodhi;
I take refuge in all the Vidyādhara and Secret Honored Ones, Paying respectful homage with the purity of the three karmas.
The mantra for the expedient means of prostration is as follows; employ the Earth-Holding Mudrā:
Oṃ namas sarvatathāgatebhyo gaye mivakṣipta prabhaṇaṃdanakāruṇi. Placing the right knee upon the ground, one repents of prior transgressions:
"I have committed manifold sins through the actions of body, speech, and mind; because my mind was shrouded by greed, hatred, and delusion."
Toward the Buddha’s True Dharma and the Sangha of Sages, my parents, my two teachers, and spiritual friends,
as well as toward immeasurable sentient beings throughout the beginningless cycle of birth and death,
I have committed countless and most grievous offenses. Now, in the presence of the Buddhas currently residing in the ten directions, I confess them all.
"I repent all [of these] and shall not commit them again.
The mantra for the expedient means of expiating transgressions is as follows, using the Great Wisdom Sword Seal:
"I take refuge in the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time, and in the treasury of the True Dharma of the three kinds of eternal bodies."
"To the assembly of the secret Bodhicitta of supreme vows, I now take refuge in all of them with perfect sincerity.
The mantra for the skillful means of taking refuge is used with the universal mudrā:
"I purify this body, free from all defilements, Along with the bodies, speech, and minds of the three times."
Exceeding the number of atoms in oceans of lands, I offer them to all the Tathāgatas.
The mantra for the skillful means of offering the body, using the single-pronged vajra mudrā, is as follows:
"The jewel of the supreme vow of the pure bodhicitta, I now arouse it to deliver all living beings."

Enveloped by the accumulation of birth, suffering, and the like, and with bodies harmed by ignorance, you rescue, gather, and provide refuge for them to bring about liberation; may you always benefit all sentient beings.
The mantra for generating the bodhicitta is performed with the vajra-bond mudrā:
"All those who are the Perfectly Enlightened Ones throughout all worlds in the ten directions,
With their various skillful expressions of thought— May the Buddhas extensively deliver all living beings."
"Whatever measure of meritorious deeds and the like have been performed, I now rejoice in them all.
The mantra for this is: "With palms joined in homage, I now entreat all the Tathāgatas and the Bodhisattvas, the secret saviors of the world:"
"I only pray that throughout the realms of the ten directions, you will always let fall the rain of Dharma from great clouds.
The mantra for this exhortation is recited with palms joined in homage:
"May those dwelling as ordinary beings quickly cast off this body, which is a collection of manifold sufferings."
"One shall attain the stainless state, abiding securely in the pure body of the Dharmadhātu.
The mantra for invoking the Dharmakāya is as follows, employing the external binding with the wind-hook:
"Whatever wholesome karmas have been cultivated, for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings..."
I now dedicate all of this correctly, To eliminate the suffering of birth and death and reach Bodhi.
The mantra for dedication uses the Universal Seal:
To cause body and mind to be entirely purified, Out of compassion, to rescue and protect oneself and others.
The nature of mind is thus free from all defilements; the body sits at ease as appropriate.
Next, one binds the samaya, re-enters the arising of the dharmadhātu, dons the armor of the sattva, and desires to purify the realm of sentient beings.
First, through the arising of the Dharmadhātu, place the mudrā and mantra at the position of the heart;
contemplate clearly the wisdom of self-nature, wherein the syllable RA exists within the essence,
such that it becomes the fire of wisdom pervading the entire body, whereby all defilements become unfindable.
The Buddha taught that among fires this is supreme:
the triangular fire-light arises like the fierce blaze of the sun’s radiance. First it burns away false discrimination;
then, when the karma of the *ālayavijñāna* is exhausted, so too are the great elements, the aggregates, the sense-bases, and the realms.
Causing all to be quiescent by nature.
With both hands in vajra-fists, extend the wind-wheels (the index fingers); this is called the Seal of the Pure Dharma Realm (*dharmadhātu-viśuddha-mudrā*).
Its mantra is as follows:
Having recited that vidyā three times, one raises the mudrā at the crown of the head and gradually brings it down to the feet;
this can incinerate the aggregates and the four great elements.
All phenomena are fundamentally unarisen, for their intrinsic nature is quiescent.
This is the Ground of the Pure Mind; therefore, it is called the "Burning of Letters.
Having incinerated the realm of sentient beings, all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen, and the nature of the mind is inherently pure.
Next, one contemplates the wheel of the syllable A, empowered by all Buddhas;
its color is like a mass of gold, its form is universally square and equal,
and its nature is indestructible— this is called the Vajra Earth Wheel.
Empowering the lower body from the feet to the navel is called the yoga seat,
which is the Vajra-jewel realm.
Its mantra is as follows:
Homage to the One: Āḥ.
The mudrā is like Vajramati.
Through the power of the mantra and mudrā, one is empowered and becomes a yogin.
Without destroying the vajra-seat,
one next contemplates the vajra-wisdom; its radiance illuminates sentient beings,
causing them all to attain this same stage.
The syllable VAṂ is produced, its characteristic wisdom located at the navel;
white in color and perfectly luminous, like the moonlight in its ninth stage amidst a light mist,
it flows forth as a stream of nectar-water.
It moistens and nourishes the realm of sentient beings, and is thus called the "Wheel of Concentration Water.
It is empowered at the site of the navel, and is therefore named the "Water of Great Compassion.
Its mantra is as follows:
Homage to No. 1, Vī.
The mudrā is the same as that of the lotus.
By the power of this mantra and mudrā, and through the majesty of its empowerment, one attains the samādhi of Great Compassion.
Next, one contemplates the samādhi of great compassion;
its essence is identical to the wisdom of self-nature, luminous and pure, fundamentally free from defilement.
It can give rise to the syllable *laṃ*, red in color like the radiance of the sun, triangular and emitting majestic flames.
It is named the Wheel of Wisdom Fire, capable of removing defilements and obscurations.
Because it is empowered within the state of the mind, it is called the Majestic Power of Wisdom Fire.
Its mantra is as follows:
Homage to the One: Raṃ.
The mudrā is the same as that of the Great Sword of Wisdom.
By the power of this mudrā and mantra, it is empowered to become the nature of the Great Reality-Mark Fire-Wheel.
Next, one contemplates the wind of self-nature; stirred by the blazing flames of wisdom-light, it gives rise to the syllable HAṂ.
Its form is like a half-moon disc, dark blue-black and generating fierce wrath;
it wafts and moves through the realms of the ten directions.
The causes, effects, and karmas of sentient beings are all devoid of intrinsic nature;
since their nature is fundamentally neither bound nor liberated, they constitute the wind-circle of liberation.
With empowerment centered between the eyebrows, one is able to destroy all evil māras.
Therefore, it is named the Wind of Liberation.
Its mantra is: Namo ekam hūṃ.
The mudrā is the same as that for turning the wheel of Dharma.
Through the power of the mudrā-mantra, the wind-wheel of liberation is formed.
Next, one contemplates the nature of liberation: its essence is empty, yet it contains all colors.
From the void of true emptiness arises the syllable *kha*; visualize it placed upon the crown of the head.
Its color is dark blue and its form is all-pervasive; it is perfectly round and extends throughout the ten directions.
This is called the Great Wheel of Emptiness, which is entirely without obstruction.
The mantra for that is:
*Namo ekam* (Homage to the One), followed by *Khaṃ*.
The mudrā is called the Honored Emptiness (*Uṣṇīṣavijayā*).
Through the power of mantras and mudrās, they are empowered to be equal to the dharmadhātu.
At that time, the World-Honored One entered the samādhi of Subduing the Four Māras and spoke the Universal Mudrā of Fulfillment through its phrases.
The five locations.
Their mantra is as follows:
"By the power of the mantra and the mudrā, one is able to subdue the four māras."
Through the death of the five aggregates of affliction, one is liberated from the six realms;
fulfilling all-encompassing wisdom, one purifies the five aggregates and the four great elements to realize the fivefold Dharma-body.
Next, bind the samaya; again enter the Dharmadhātusaṃbhava and don the armor of the sattva.
As in the previous Dharmadhātusaṃbhava, the mudrā is rotated to the position of the heart.
Having recited that vidyā three times, one should use the mudrā to visualize the burning away of earth,
water, fire, wind, and all conditioned phenomena, so that everything becomes the unconditioned realm of space like the conflagration at the end of an eon.
Permanently free from the faults of the conditioned, Immovable and identical to the great void, The station of the Buddhas of the ten directions; Therefore, it is named the Pure Two Realms.
The mantra for this is:
Homage to the One: *Raṃ*.
The mantra practitioner contemplates that the realm of sentient beings is identical to the great void;
recollecting again the emptiness of their fundamental nature, they establish the unconditioned realm.
They purify the Buddha-lands and enter the Abode of the Dharma-realm; through the Samādhi of the Treasury of Adornments,
they manifest within the Dharma-realm because its adornments are inexhaustible.
By means of the gateway of mantra practice, one delivers the multitudes of all realms without exception.
Next, one should mindfully hold the earth and awaken the Earth Deity.
The verse for awakening the Earth Deity is as follows: With the Samādhi-hand holding the Wisdom-vajra at the heart, the Wisdom-hand’s five wheels press upon the ground:
O Devaputra, you who protect us, Having practiced sublime conduct under the Buddhas, the Guides,
And purified the stages and the perfections,
Just as the Lion of the Śākyas, the Savior of the World, destroyed the hosts of Māra.
I too have subdued Māra and uttered this verse of origination, which can produce the various forms corresponding to their kinds—
the dharmic characteristics of all phenomena.
The World-Saviors, the Pratyekabuddhas, the diligent and courageous assembly of Bodhisattvas,
and likewise the Benevolent Honored One—
these are established in succession; so too are all phenomena such as arising and abiding.
Thus it arises eternally;
free from lack of wisdom and doubt, because one contemplates this path,
the Perfectly Enlightened Ones have taught it.
The unconditioned dharmas of intrinsic nature, The wisdom of the five wheels and the three samādhis,
are identical to the pure Dharma-realm.
Contemplating the ten phrases of dependent origination, One knows that the aggregates are fundamentally unborn.
Then there is no longer any cessation.
Within this state of non-arising and non-ceasing, the five wheels are successively formed, constituting the pure vessel-world.
Below, one contemplates the syllable *khaṃ*, which is perfectly full and pervades the ten directions.
Encompassing and fusing all forms, whose dark nature is unimpeded,
it is therefore called the Great Wheel of Emptiness.
Its mantra is as follows:
Homage to One. Khaṃ.
Its form is like a crescent moon turned upward; from its dark blue-black [nature] arises a great wind.
Fierce and wrathful, it possesses great power, capable of sustaining the lands of the ten directions.
Therefore, it is called the Great Wind Mandala. Its mantra is: Haṃ.
Next, visualize the syllable *raṃ* above;
from it arises a triangular mass of fierce flames like the fire at the end of an eon, hence it is called the Great Fire Wheel (*mahāgnicakra*).
Its mantra is as follows:
Lam. Next, visualize the syllable VAṂ above; its form is like nine layers of the moon, with a halo of pure white light, situated amidst a mass of mist.
It can rain down all waters, filling the great trichiliocosm;
therefore it is called the Great Water Wheel.
Its mantra is as follows:
VAṂ. Next,
visualize the letter A above it, its color like a mass of gold,
its form square and vast, beyond measurement by number or quantity.
Its nature is firm and solid, difficult to destroy; by its power it sustains lands as numerous as motes of dust—this is called the Vajra Earth-Wheel.
Its mantra is as follows:
Āḥ. The syllable of vajra-perfection, the universal clarity of the three recollections,
is empowered to become the five wheels.
The mantra for this is as follows:
By the power of the mantra and mudrā, the vessel-world is consecrated;
all five wheels are brought to perfection, just like the buddha-fields.
Adorned with various jewels, with jewel-trees abounding in flowers and fruit,
filling the entire dharma-realm, pure, most majestic, and pristine. Next,
visualize it as a great ocean, with the five treasures forming its four shores.
The ground is spread with exquisite golden sand; visualize the light-wheel of the syllable *Vī*.
Next, imagine it as a great ocean from which the water of eight virtues flows forth, filling the midst of that sea;
there, one binds the inexhaustible Ocean-Seal (*Sāgaramudrā*).
The two hands of concentration and wisdom are interlaced.
The mantra for this is:
Oṃ vimālanadhi hūṃ. By the power of this mantra and mudrā, the eight flavors shall not diminish.
Next, within that ocean, visualize with single-minded focus Mount Meru with its eight peaks; as concentration and wisdom unite internally,
they form Mount Meru.
The mantra for that is:
Oṃ aśvara hūṃ. By the power of this mantra and its mudrā, the eight peaks are all made perfect.
Next, visualize the syllable Vaṃ above, which becomes the Great Karma-cakra.
Using the Great Jewel Flower, it is firm and unshakable.
The mantra for this is: Then, one should further visualize upon the Karma-cakra the use of the Great Karma-mudrā.
Within it, one contemplates the letter A, which transforms into a white lotus;
its pedestal and filaments are all exquisitely adorned, its eight petals are vast and wide,
and it is naturally embellished with various jewels.
The mantra for that is:
"I take refuge in the One:
Āḥ. With the mudrā, perform three circumambulations, pervading the eight directions.
Visualize hundreds of thousands of lotuses, upon which the assembly of Honored Sages sits upon indestructible vajra-thrones.
Next, one should spread five colors: *raṃ*, *laṃ*, *kaṃ*, and *haṃ*.
White, red, yellow, blue, and black— these colors dye the realm of sentient beings,
causing it to become identical in color to the Dharma-realm.
Next, one arrays the vajra seals and binds the seal of vajra-wisdom.
The mantra is: Namaḥ ekahūṃ.
By the power of this mantra and mudrā, perform the vajra-mudrā three times.
Streaming forth like sparks of fire, its brilliance pervades everywhere throughout all Buddha-fields; with a mind free from doubt,
it flows out universally.
Within it is the Palace of the Dharma Realm, a vast jeweled pavilion containing the maṇḍala of Madhyamaka.
Next, one binds the seal of the Turning of the Wheel of Dharma, which is like that of the Vajraśekhara.
The mantra for that is as follows:
Having recited that mantra, seal the heart, forehead, throat, and crown of the head;
wherever the seals are applied, the Great Maṇḍala is perfected.
The sphere of mind of the Mahāsattva is called the maṇḍala;
when the practitioner abides in this state, they contemplate the letter A within a mirror,
its flaming garland exquisite and beautiful, its radiance pervading everywhere.
Illuminating the realms of sentient beings, like a convergence of a thousand flashes of lightning;
Bearing the Buddha’s exquisite form and color, dwelling deeply within the perfect mirror,
Manifesting in all directions and places, like the moon in clear water.
Manifesting universally before all beings,
within the intersection of the crown and the assembly,
one marks it with the great bindu of emptiness and contemplates the syllable *Aṃ*, which is exquisite, pure, and stainless.
Like crystal, moon, and lightning, it is described as the quiescent *dharmakāya*.
Next, one should visualize the light-wheel (*prabhāmaṇḍala*);
contemplate the syllable *va-ra*, which emits immeasurable hundreds of rays of light, forming a great wheel of perfect luminosity.
Illuminating the realms of sentient beings, even down to those as numerous as motes of dust,
their reflections enter within the circular light.
The mantra of that circular light is:
Using the Great Protection Mudrā, join the two thumbs together within the palms and extend the index fingers (vāyu-cakra).
Having recited that mantra, rotate the mudrā three times;
a circular halo will appear everywhere, and within that circle are the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
The support for all things, the yogic seat of the practitioner;
his body is identical to Vajradhara, with the syllable RAṂ as the visual faculty,
radiant like a bright lamp.
Bowing the neck slightly and lowering the head, with the tongue near the palate, one should observe the locus of the mind.
When the mind manifests in meditative equipoise (*samāhita*), it is stainless, wondrously pure,
and the perfect mirror is ever present before one.
The yogin transforms the syllables and enters the practice of the maṇḍala;
beholding the entire great assembly, he cultivates the eye of compassion and observes the realm of sentient beings.
Precisely because of this power of meditative concentration, she is called the Vidyārājñī of Unimpeded Power Who Expounds All Three Times.
Her mantra is as follows:
Reciting that mantra eight times, because there is no duality in the realm of reality, he further spoke this verse; it was likewise through the Buddha’s empowerment.
The Bodhisattva of great renown has no hindrance regarding all phenomena.
One can extinguish all sufferings by empowering oneself, as well as the Vajradharas and the foremost holders of the vajra.
"Listen attentively, Vajrapāṇi!
The maṇḍala of the wheel of syllables, through the practice of mantra cultivation,
is able to perform all the deeds of the Buddhas and universally manifest their form bodies."
At that time, Vajrapāṇi, having descended by revolving from his vajra-flower seat,
prostrated before the World-Honored One Mahāvairocana and uttered words of praise:
I take refuge in the generation of bodhicitta; I bow my head to the essence of practice, the stages, the pāramitās, and so forth.
I pay homage to those who first established [the path], and I take refuge in those who have realized emptiness.
“May the Honored Dharma King, out of compassion, protect and mind me,
and may he proclaim these words for the benefit of sentient beings,
so that the cultivation of mantras may be perfected.”
The World-Illuminating Honored One, Vairocana, addressed the Vajradhara, saying:
"He is named the Refuge of the World; his teaching of the Dharma is peerless, fundamentally quiescent, and unsurpassed."
Thus performing the empowerment, one empowers the Vajradhara and the assembly of bodhisattvas;
those who can perceive this shall see the place where the Buddha’s seat of enlightenment resides.
Free from conceptual proliferation and non-dual, one practices in accordance with yoga;
because this activity is accomplished,
all the limbs of the body manifest as syllables.
Throughout all worlds,
for pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas, as well as for all sentient beings,
they contemplate the accomplishment of siddhi, all sharing the same basis.
That seed-mantra is:
Aḥ. "Lord of Secrets!
The Universal Manifestation of the Form Body, this is the heart-mind of all Buddhas;
the secret within secrets, born from the Womb of Great Compassion,
the King of the Great Maṇḍala, wherein the stations of the holy deities are laid out.
The practice of the supernatural powers of samādhi:
Contemplating the letter A within a mirror, it emits pure and wondrous light;
this light universally appears within a circular halo, with thousands of worlds serving as its increasing count.
From the radiance of the wheel of flames,
he becomes the Great Illuminator (Mahāvairocana). The Teacher, having attained perfect enlightenment,
is surrounded by the seed-syllables of the eight maṇḍalas.
Each holding their respective insignia, they bring awakening according to individual dispositions;
their bodies and speech pervade all things.
With the pure golden hue of Jambudvīpa, they appear in accordance with the world.
Seated cross-legged upon a lotus, in meditative equipoise free from all poisons;
his body draped in fine silk and gauze garments, his hair bound in a topknot crown;
through the gateway of syllables he turns to Buddhahood, universally benefiting all sentient beings.
The yogi observes one body, two bodies,
and even immeasurable bodies; each abiding in samādhi,
all receive the Buddha’s transformation, vowing to be born in the Flower Treasury Ocean.
Entering together into a single essence, they form the great maṇḍala.
Next, one contemplates the Vast Jewel Pavilion of Ākāśagarbha;
within this great jewel pavilion, jeweled pillars stand in orderly rows.
Everywhere there are various banners and canopies, interlaced with strings of pearls and the like;
exquisite jeweled robes hang down, and clouds of incense and flowers,
as well as clouds of various jewels, are spread all around, raining down clouds of diverse blossoms everywhere.
A profusion of ornaments adorns the ground, while beloved melodies harmonize as various musical instruments are played.
The auspicious vase and the argha-offering vessel stand ready, and the king of jewel-trees is in full bloom.
Illuminated by mani-lamps,
with sovereign ladies, The Buddha’s perfections and so forth,
the wondrously adorned flowers of enlightenment, And skillful means manifesting various performances.
Chanting the sublime sound of the Dharma, I offer clouds of worship;
in each ocean-like assembly of Buddhas, I make offerings to all the Tathāgatas and the host of Vajra Bodhisattvas through the power of my merit.
Through the power of the Tathāgata’s empowerment and the power of the dharmadhātu,
one dwells making universal offerings; this is the consort Ākāśagarbha with the mudrā of the vajra-palms joined.
The mantra is as follows:
"I respectfully invite the World-Honored One, Vairocana, And all Tathāgatas from the oceans of realms and lands,
Along with the assembly of Bodhisattvas, Vajras, and Śrāvakas, To gather like vast clouds within this great pavilion."
The infinite assembly of noble ones all bear witness: I now purify the two realms as the Buddha does;

Having perfected the body and established the maṇḍala, With its various adornments now complete, May you descend out of compassion and your original vows; I pray that the noble assembly fulfills their fundamental aspirations.
At that time, the Bhagavān immediately entered the samādhi of the Power of Harmlessness toward the Body.
Abiding in this concentration, he proclaimed the Vidyārājñī of the Pledge-Entry of All Tathāgatas, which is all-pervasive, unimpeded, and possesses the three incomparable powers.
Regarding this mudrā: one should form an open-hollowed joined-palms gesture with the hands of concentration and wisdom, joining the two space-wheels (thumbs) side by side and holding them upright.
The verse says:
"This is the Great Seal of all Buddhas, The savior of the world."
The Samaya of Perfect Enlightenment abides in this mudrā.
Its mantra is as follows:
(1) *asame*, (2) *tariṣame*, (3) *samaye*, (4) *svāhā*. "O Lord of Secrets!"
"Such a consort manifests the ground of all Tathāgatas, which does not transcend the perfection of the ground that fulfills the realm of the three dharmas.

Then, forming fists with the hands of concentration and wisdom, placing the space-wheel (thumb) within the palms, and extending the two wind-wheels (index fingers), this is the Seal of the Pure Dharma-realm.
The mantra for that is:

first, *ṛṃ dharmadhātu*; second, *svāhā svāhā hūṃ*. Third, again with the hands of concentration and wisdom, all five wheels are equalized and interlaced with one another, while the two space-wheels (thumbs) are both directed toward each other.
The verse says:
This is called the Supreme Vow, the Auspicious Dharma-Wheel Seal;
the Refuges of the World, the Saviors of the World, all turn the Wheel of Dharma.
The mantra for this is as follows:
By the power of the mantra and the mudrā,
one should abide in meditative equipoise and clearly contemplate that this body of mine is indeed Vajrapāṇi.
Innumerable celestial Māras and others—whosoever beholds them, they are like Vajrasattva; do not give rise to a mind of doubt.
Next, one should don the armor; one should contemplate the garments being worn.
Flames of light arise from his entire body, which he uses to adorn his form;
all Māras who act as obstacles, as well as other beings of evil intent,
scatter in the four directions upon seeing him.
The two wind-wheels of śamatha and vipaśyanā support the fire-wheel above;
the two voids are naturally aligned within the palms—
this is the Vajra Armor Seal.
Through the power of the mantra and mudrā, one should visualize the stainless syllable.
That mantra is as follows:
Through the power of the mantra and mudrā, one should imagine placing the seals at the five locations.
At the forehead, left and right, the heart, and the throat, the light of samādhi pervades the entire body;
even the celestial Māras cannot destroy it.
Next, bind the Dharmadhātujāta mudrā and visualize a white syllable RAṂ.
Adorned with the dot of emptiness, like a bright jewel in a topknot placed upon the crown of the head;
whatever mass of sinful defilements has been accumulated throughout a hundred eons is entirely extinguished by this.
The winds of concentration and wisdom are perfected; the seal is identical to that which arises from the Dharma-realm.
Its mantra is: RAṂ.
The mantra is identical to the Dharma-realm; immeasurable multitudes of sins are eliminated.
Before long, one shall achieve accomplishment and abide on the stage of non-retrogression.
In all places that are defiled by contact, one should apply this gateway of syllables (akṣaramukha).
Red in color and endowed with majestic radiance, it is completely encircled by a wreath of flames.

Furthermore, with the hands of concentration and wisdom, perform the *añjali* of refuge; join the two *vāyu-cakras* (ring fingers) together and place the two *ākāśa-cakras* (thumbs) upon them, forming the shape of a *karkaṭaka* (crab).
The verse says:
This seal of the great sword of wisdom was taught by all Buddhas;
it is able to sever all views, namely, the innate view of a self-body.
The mantra for that is as follows:

1. *Mahā-khaḍga-virāja* 2. *Dharma-sannāha-saṃrakṣaka* 3. *Sattvārtha-niścitānugata* 4. *Tathāgata-dharmatā-anupraviṣṭa* 5. *Vira-gadha-manīṣita hūṃ* Furthermore, with the hands of Samādhi and Prajñā joined in the hollow-palms gesture (*añjali*), bend the two index fingers (*vāyu*) to encircle the two thumbs (*ākāśa-cakra*), forming a shape like a conch shell (*śaṅkha*).
The verse says:
With the auspicious Dharma-conch mudrā, the Buddhas, teachers of the world,

One reaches the state of quiescent nirvāṇa.
The mantra for this is as follows:

First, "Darkness" (Aṃ); then, join the hands of concentration and wisdom together, spreading them wide like a *kaṅka* bird. Second, hold the two earth-wheels (*pṛthivī-maṇḍala*) and the two space-wheels (*ākāśa-maṇḍala*) together, while the fire-wheel (*tejas-maṇḍala*) and wind-wheel (*vāyu-maṇḍala*) are brought into union.
The verse says:
Auspiciously, may the lotus of aspiration, the Buddhas who save the world, upon the indestructible vajra seat, awaken; this is called Buddhahood.
Bodhi and the sons of the Buddha are all born from this. The mantra is: *Āḥ*.

Furthermore, with the hands of Samādhi and Prajñā, form fists by turning the five wheels inward. Raise the fire wheel (the thumbs) and extend the two wind wheels (the index fingers), bending them into the shape of hooks and holding them at the side. Align the space wheel (the little fingers) and the earth wheel (the ring fingers) straight upward, and interlace the water wheels (the middle fingers) like a *vajra*.
The verse says:
The seal of the great vajra wisdom can destroy the city of ignorance;
it awakens those who sleep, and neither gods nor humans can destroy it.
The mantra for that is: *Namaḥ samantavajrāya hūṃ*.

Furthermore, with the hands of Samādhi and Prajñā, form fists by drawing the five fingers inward; extend the fire-fingers (the middle fingers), place the two wind-fingers (the index fingers) beside them, and bend the two space-fingers (the thumbs) so they touch each other.
The verse says:
This mudrā is the Mahāmudrā, known as the Tathāgata-ūṣṇīṣa;

The mantra for that is:

The verse says:
This is called the Uṣṇīṣa-garbha, the Buddha’s Seal of Ever-Fulfilling Wishes;
by merely forming this seal, one becomes equal to the Supreme among Men.
Its mantra is as follows:

First, quickly call out "A" and "Hañja," and quickly call out "Dhū," while remaining in the yoga posture and holding the bowl in accordance with the ritual. With both the wisdom hand and the concentration hand together at the navel, this is called the Great Bowl Seal of Śākyamuni.

Then, with the wisdom hand (*jñānahasta*) turned upward, one forms the gesture of granting fearlessness (*abhayamudrā*).
The verse says:
One who is able to bestow fearlessness upon all classes of sentient beings,

Its mantra is as follows:
1. *Sarvatha* 2. *Ira ira* 3. *Peyanaśana* 4. *Svāhā* Next, with the wisdom hand, extend it downward to form the gesture of granting boons (*varada-mudrā*).
The verse says:
This Seal of Granting Wishes was taught by the Refuge of the World;

The mantra for that is:
*Vāranavajratmakā svāhā*. Then, with the hand of wisdom, form a fist and extend the wind-wheel (the index finger) in the form of Vidyujjvālākarālī, abiding in meditative equipoise (*samādhi*).
The verse says:
By means of this Great Seal, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Protectors,

By binding this mudrā, the hosts of great and evil māras,
as well as all other obstructors, will flee in dispersal without a doubt.
The mantra for that is:

1. *Mahā-mārāvati* (with the final syllable pronounced with the *tingyi* [dental] retroflex). 2. *Narṣa-vāruṇpave*. 3. *Mahā-maitry-abhyudgate*. 4. *Svāhā*. Next, form a fist with the hand of wisdom (*prajñā-hasta*) and extend the fire-wheel (*tejas-tarjanī*) and water-wheel (*ap-śūlapāṇi*).
The verse says:
This is called the eye of all Buddhas, the eye born of compassion for the world’s refuge.
By visualizing it as being placed within the field of vision, the wise attain the Buddha-eye.
The mantra for that is:

(1) *Āgana-varāṅkṣaṇe*; (2) *Karūṇāmaya*; (3) *Tathāgatadhātu*; (4) *Svāhā*. Next, join the hands of concentration and wisdom together to form a fist; extend the wind-wheel (the index finger) of the wisdom hand and bend its third joint so that it resembles a ring.
The verse says:
Such is called the Hook Seal (Aṅkuśa-mudrā);
by it, all the Buddhas, the Saviors of the World, who abide on the ten stages, are summoned and gathered together.
For those with the great mind of bodhicitta and for sentient beings of evil intent, the mantra is as follows: 1.

Oṃ sarvatrāpratihatatejāye 2. tathāgataguhye 3. mādicaryāparipūrakāya 4. svāhā Furthermore, with the hands of concentration and wisdom, form fists by turning the five fingers inward, then extend the wind-fingers (index fingers) so that their tips meet in a circular shape.
The verse says:
This seal of the supreme wish-granting lasso destroys all who commit evil;
when bound by the mantra-practitioner, it is able to bind all that is unwholesome.
The mantra is as follows:

1. *He he mahābhaṣa* 2. *Pra-sāraṇāya* 3. *Sattvadhātu* 4. *Vimohaka* 5. *Tathāgatadhimuktinirjāta* 6. *Svāhā* Immediately following this, extend the fire-finger (*anāmikā*) of the previously described hook-seal (*ākarṣaṇamudrā*) and slightly bend it; this is the heart-seal (*hṛdayamudrā*) of all Tathāgatas.
The mantra for that is:
(1) *jraṃ*, (2) *upava*, (3) *svāhā*. Furthermore, by extending the water-wheel fingers (*tarjanī*) of this mudrā and holding them upright, it is called the Tathāgata Navel Mudrā.
The mantra for this is:

(1) *amṛtodbhava*, (2) *svāhā*. Using this same mudrā, extend the earth-touching finger (*pṛthivī-lāñchana*) straight out while keeping the other fingers upright; this is called the Tathāgata Waist Mudrā.
The mantra for this is:

(1) *tathāgata-svabhāvāḥ*; (2) *svāhā*. Furthermore, with the hands of concentration and wisdom joined in the hollow-palms gesture (*śūnyatā-muṣṭi*), bend the two wind-wheels (*anāmikā*) inward; slightly bend the two earth-wheels (*kaniṣṭhikā*) and extend the fire-wheels (*tarjanī*). This is the Tathāgatagarbha Mudrā.
The mantra for that is:
*Namaḥ sarvatathāgatebhyo raṃ raṃ hūṃ hūṃ svāhā*. Next, bind the two protective gates.
Then, with this very mudrā, one disperses the water-wheel and places it facing upward;

Then the Buddha arose from samādhi and, emitting a voice that pervaded the entire dharma-realm of all Tathāgatas and took pity upon the realm of sentient beings without exception, he spoke this Great Power Great Protection Vidyārājñī.

Then, using the previously mentioned Great Boundary Seal (*mahā-sīmā-mudrā*), join the two fire-wheels (*tejas-tarjanī*) by hooking and bending them together, and extend the wind-wheels (*vāyu-aṅguṣṭha*). This is called the "Unbearable Great Protection Seal" (*asahya-mahārakṣa-mudrā*). Its mantra is as follows:

For the eastern direction, perform the Fearless Protection Seal (*abhaya-rakṣā-mudrā*) and hold the staff seal; the syllable is *va*. For the northern direction, perform the Destruction of All Terrors Great Protection Seal and hold the sword seal; the syllable is *ma*. For the western direction, perform the Difficult-to-Conquer Great Protection Seal and hold the sword seal; the syllable is *sa*. *Traṭa traṭa* (10) *aprati-hate* (11) *svāhā*.
As soon as this vidyā had been spoken, the entire buddha-field shook in six ways.
All the bodhisattvas, having attained what they had never experienced before, opened their eyes wide and, in the presence of all the Buddhas, spoke these verses with pleasing words:
“The Buddhas are most rare and marvelous, Who have taught this protection of great power;
Sustained by all the Buddhas, The city walls and moats are all firm and secure.
Because the protective mind abides therein, All those who would create obstacles—”
The Vināyakas and other rākṣasas of hideous form all retreat and disperse by the power of reciting the mantra.
Next, one should bind the seal and recite the vidyā of Acala to perform empowerment.
That which is offered removes defilement, dispels obstacles, manifests radiance,
and increases great majestic power.
The mantra for this is as follows:

*Namo samantavajrāṇāṃ haṃ khaṃ.* Next, bind the mudrā for the *arghya* perfumed water: with both hands, hold the *arghya* vessel of perfumed water and visualize bathing the assembly of all noble ones; one should then make the five great vows.
The mantra for that is as follows:
Next, form the mudrā of the scented unguent:
clench the left hand into the fist at the wrist with the right, extend the five fingers of the right hand upward with the palm facing out, and assume the gesture of granting fearlessness.
The mantra for that is as follows:
Having recited that mantra, visualize clouds and oceans of incense-paste vessels flowing forth from the mudrā,
filling the entirety of space and the dharma-realm.
In the great ocean-like assemblies of dust-mote lands, one makes offerings to each and every Honored One.
Next, bind the Tathāgata-seat mudrā, which is identical to that of the Flower-seat mudrā.
Its mantra is as follows:
Seated as the Honored One among all the Sages, upon the indestructible Vajra-seat,
may all sentient beings of the Dharma-realm likewise sit upon the seat of the emptiness of phenomena.
At that time, the Bhagavat, through the empowerment of the vast Dharma-realm, immediately entered the Samādhi of the Matrix of the Dharma-realm.
Emerging from this samādhi, he spoke on entering the Buddha-samaya.
That mantra is as follows:
"By correctly demonstrating the samaya, one is able to universally increase [all virtues]."
All classes of sentient beings shall attain siddhi;
may their supreme aspirations be swiftly fulfilled, through the Great Lord of Mantras and all the Vidyās who are filled with joy.
Next, form the mudrā for offering flowers: Interlace the fingers of concentration and wisdom within;
curl the two wind-wheels (index fingers) into circles, their tips leaning against one another;
and place the two space-wheels (thumbs) alongside the sides of the wind-wheels.
The mantra for this is:
Contemplating the flow forth from the seal, the flowers of the seven untainted factors of enlightenment arise as a vast ocean of various flower-clouds, pervading and filling the entire Dharma-realm.
The assembly of Buddha-fields as numerous as motes of dust becomes a vast and magnificent offering.

Next, bind the incense-offering mudrā: join the fingers of wisdom and concentration back-to-back, support the two wind-wheels (the little fingers) against each other at their sides, and extend the two space-wheels (the thumbs).
Press the sides of the two wind-wheels (index fingers).
The mantra for that is as follows:
Having recited that mantra, visualize it flowing forth from the mudrā.
The incense smoke burns, forming clouds and seas that pervade the entirety of empty space;
before each and every assembly of sages within the oceans of micro-dust worlds,
various kinds of incense are offered as worship, all entering together into the essence of the Dharma-realm.
Next, bind the food and drink mudrā: join the hands of concentration and wisdom at the heart, form the seal, and perform the visualization.
The mantra for this is as follows:
Having recited that mantra, clouds of immeasurable food and drink pervade the entirety of space;
before each and every assembly of sages within buddha-fields as numerous as motes of dust,
they are offered as vast and magnificent offerings.
Feeding on the joy of Dharma and the delight of dhyāna, next one binds the Lamp-Light Mudrā: the Wisdom-Wing forms a fist;
the Wind-wheel (ring finger) entwines the Fire-wheel (middle finger); the Space-finger (thumb) presses upon the Water and Earth armors (index and little fingers).
The fire-wheel is straight and upright.
Its mantra is as follows:
Having recited that mantra, it illuminates while rotating to the right.
Flowing forth from the seal, an infinite ocean of clouds of lamps pervades the entirety of empty space; within every atom of all lands,
each lamp is vast and great, illuminating the ocean-like assemblies of Buddhas.
Next, one contemplates the Vast and Great Jewel Pavilion of Ākāśagarbha;
within this great jewel pavilion, jewel pillars stand in orderly rows,
with various banners and canopies everywhere, and pearl garlands interlaced throughout.
Precious, wondrous robes hang suspended down;
clouds of fragrant flowers and clouds of various jewels are spread all around.
Clouds of diverse blossoms rain down everywhere, scattering profusely to adorn the ground, while harmonious melodies of beloved sounds resound.
And let various musical instruments be played.
Within the altar, one should visualize the pure and wondrous, the auspicious vase and the argha-offering.
The king of jewel-trees is in full bloom, illuminated by mani-lamps.
The sovereign ladies, the Buddha’s perfections and so forth,
are the exquisite flowers of the adornment of enlightenment; through skillful means they perform various arts,
singing the melodies of the sublime Dharma.
In each and every ocean-like assembly of Buddhas, I make offerings to all the Tathāgatas,
And to the hosts of Bodhisattvas and Vajradharas.

Furthermore, with the hands of concentration and wisdom joined in the hollow-palms gesture (*khaṭakāmudrā*), one holds the two wind-wheels (*vāyu-maṇḍala*) against the sides of the fire-wheel (*tejo-maṇḍala*); this is called the "Tathāgata-coming-armour" (*tathāgatāgata-kavaca*).
To seal those mantras, one should apply seals to five locations: the forehead, the right and left shoulders, the heart, and the throat:

(1) *praṇava*, (2) *vajrajvala*, (3) *viśphura hūṃ*. Furthermore, according to the previous procedure for the Great Power Great Protection Seal, join the thumbs (*ākāśa-cakra*) together within the palms and extend the index fingers (*vāyu-cakra*); this is called the Tathāgata Universal Radiance Seal (*tathāgata-samantaprabhā-mudrā*).
The mantra for that is:

(1) *jvala-mariṇi*, (2) *tathāgata-ṛddhi*, *svāhā*. Again, following the previous procedure, form the *kavaca* (armor) mudrā, but place the two thumbs inside; this is called the Tathāgata’s Tongue-mark Mudrā.

The mantra is as follows: (1) *tathāgata-arhate*; (2) *sadya-dharma-pratisthita*; (3) *svāhā*. This is called the Seal of the Tathāgata’s Gate of Speech (*Tathāgatavāgmukha-mudrā*).
The mantra for this is:

(1) *tathāgata-mahāvajratra*, (2) *viśvājñānam āhūya*, (3) *svāhā*. Furthermore, following the previous method, form the Gate Seal (*vākyamudrā*): bend the two wind-wheels (the index fingers) into the palms and place them beside the space-wheels (the thumbs); this is called the Tathāgata-tooth seal (*tathāgatadaṃṣṭramudrā*).
The mantra is as follows: (1) *tathāgata-neṣṭhara*;

(2) *rasa-rasa-gara*; (3) *saṃpravāka*; (4) *sarva-tathāgata*; (5) *viśaya-sambhava*; (6) *svāhā*. Again, following the previous method for the tooth mudrā, place the two *vāyu-maṇḍalas* (index fingers) upward and bend the third phalanges; this is called the Tathāgata-vaiśāradya-mudrā.
The mantra is as follows:

(1) *arjita-nābuda*, (2) *rūpavatsamanta-prabhāta*, (3) *viśuddha-svabhāva*, (4) *svāhā*. Bend the two earth-wheels (*tarjanīs*) and the two space-wheels (*aṅguṣṭhas*) inward so that they touch; this is the Tathāgata’s Seal of Holding the Ten Powers (*daśabala*).
The mantra for this is: first, *naśyamaṃlagadara*;

second, *hūṃ*; third, *jñāṃ*; third, *svāhā*. The mantra is as follows: (1) *tathāgata-samṛddhi*;

(2) *sattva-hetv-abhyudgata*; (3) *gagana-sam-sama*; (4) *svāhā*. The mantra is as follows:

(1) *Sarvadharmasamatabhāva*; (2) *Tathāgatānutpāda*; (3) *Svāhā*. At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva immediately entered the Buddha-realm Adornment Samādhi; contemplating the letter *A* as his essence, he became identical with the conduct of Samantabhadra.

To the east of the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana is a great white lotus pedestal.
Within a perfectly pure lunar disc, there appears internally the color of a conch shell;
one contemplates the dharma-gate of the syllable *khaṃ*.
From its triangular form, light rays are emitted, all of which are brilliant white, encircled by vajra seals.
From that King of Mantras, light radiates all around and flows forth everywhere;
holding this subdues the four Māras,

The mind of all those Buddhas is called Mahāvīra.

In the northern quarter, upon a great lotus pedestal, visualize the syllable *Vaṃ* with its circle of light.

Abiding in the samādhi of right reception, She is named Ākāśanetra (Space-Eye).

Smiling, seated upon a white lotus, with Amitāyus appearing upon his crown,

The mantra for this is as follows:
Next, within the flower pedestal on the left, one contemplates the dharma-gate of the syllable *Haṃ*,

With the color of the morning sun’s radiance, adorned with white lotuses,

Her mantra is as follows:

To the right of Vajrapāṇi, holding the chain (śaṅkhalā).

The mantra for this is as follows:
To the left, within a red lotus, visualize the syllable *Aṃ* with its circle of light;

Abiding in the indestructible vajra-samādhi, he spoke this mantra.

To the right of the Honored One Kṣitigarbha, visualize clearly within a precious flower.

Form the wisdom-fist and extend the water-wheel (ring finger).

(1) *daraṇi dara*, (2) *svāhā*. Within the precious lotus, visualize the syllable *haṃ* surrounded by a circle of light.
Transforming into the Jewel-Seal Hand, it is like the previous five-pronged seal.

the secret mudrā is identical to that of Maitreya, with the two voids entering the palms.

The mantra for that is as follows:
Next, within the left lotus, contemplate the dharma-gate of the syllable *tlaṃ*.
All phenomena are as they originally were; it is the body of intrinsic nature, free from defilement.
Light pervades the ten directions, transforming into a mass of fire upon the crown.
The mudrā is the same as that of the Buddha-ūṣṇīṣa.

The nature of the central dharmadhātu, A perfectly luminous and vast wheel.
Within the wheel, the letter A revolves, forming the body of the Great Dharma-realm;

Without giving rise to doubt or hesitation, take up that single-mindedness;

One hundred or one thousand, with the count reaching three lakṣas;

Like the orb of the sun appearing everywhere, for the sake of benefiting sentient beings;

Untie them at the crown of the head, each according to its proper place,

The sattva dons the armor and is protected by the three mudrās and the rest.

The Avataṃsaka, the Nirvāṇa, the Laṅkāvatāra, the Saṃdhinirmocana, and so forth— may I,

The Vast Ritual Manual of the Mahāvairocana Sūtra, Volume II. This teaching was transmitted from Mahāvairocana to Vajrapāṇi; Vajrapāṇi subsequently transmitted it to the ācārya Dharmakūṭa of Nālandā Monastery; and the ācārya Dharmakūṭa subsequently entrusted it to the Tripiṭaka Master Śubhakarasiṃha of the Śākya clan, a member of the royal lineage of Central India.

The Tripiṭaka Master Śubhakarasiṃha arrived in this country during the Kaiyuan era; serving as the Great State Preceptor during the reign of Emperor Xuanzong, he transmitted the Dharma and conferred empowerment.

He subsequently entrusted it to the Silla monk, Acharya Xuanchao; Acharya Xuanchao in turn entrusted it to the monk of the Capital’s Qinglong Monastery, Acharya Huiguo; and Acharya Huiguo in turn entrusted it to the monk Acharya Faron.

On the seventh day of the third month in the eighth year of the Taika era, the year of Jiayin (734 CE), this was entrusted to the monks of the Five Divisions who maintain the recitations at Eizan-ji Temple.

The three fascicles of the *Mahāvairocana-vistara-vidhi* were translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śubhakarasiṃha; these were brought back [to Japan] at the request of the Sōjō (Chief Abbot) Enchō of this school.
The present edition appears to have been left uncorrected, and no alternative version exists for collation.

However, since the texts cited by An’nen, Shari, Hōzan, Gōji, and others are entirely identical to this one, it is certain that this was the ritual manual as it originally stood, unrefined. Therefore, I have now punctuated it and occasionally preserved both possible readings.
Furthermore, to prevent those who are arrogant regarding the Dharma from frequently causing omissions or errors, I have marked the transmitted teachings to indicate them.
As for all other corrections, I have placed annotations at their heads, awaiting future sages in the hope that they will rectify them.
Recorded with reverence by the śramaṇa Huiguang at Lingyun Monastery on the eighth day of the first month of the first year of the Zhengde era, the Xinmao year.
